title: Apple Watch Blood Oxygen reading leading to diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary embolism
summary: Apple Watch Series 7 SpO2 of 88% prompted CT angiography that found pulmonary embolism; anticoagulated and discharged (Japan).
account: A case appeared online on 5 September 2022 in QJM (event date not reported). A 50-year-old woman who recently had COVID-19 was referred to the authors' hospital (Oita University, Yufu, Japan) for assessment of dyspnea. Hospital pulse oximetry read 97%, but her Apple Watch Series 7 had shown 88% oxygen saturation in the early morning. Prompted by the watch reading, clinicians did emergent computed tomography (CT) angiography. It showed filling defects in multiple pulmonary artery branches, confirming pulmonary embolism with bilateral deep venous thrombosis (DVT). She was treated with a direct oral anticoagulant, oxygen was stopped on day 6 and she was discharged on day 15. The authors state the watch's low reading led to the diagnosis.
purpose: The Blood Oxygen app measures oxygen saturation for general wellness and is not intended for medical diagnosis. Detecting a pulmonary embolism was not what it was built to do.
model_version: Apple Watch Series 7 (event); Series 6 in echo

ratings.reason: A pulmonary embolism with bilateral DVT was diagnosed and anticoagulated after hospital oximetry had been normal. A life-changing benefit, though the source does not establish that death was imminent.

ai_role.statement: The watch's pulse-oximetry algorithm produced the 88% reading on the patient's watch. The letter does not say who reported it to the clinicians and describes no automatic alert. Clinicians chose to perform CT angiography because of that reading and state that it led to the diagnosis.

evidence.title: Smartwatch Detection of Refractory Hypoxemia in Phenazopyridine-Induced Methemoglobinemia
evidence.quote: The day before presentation, she was walking in the mall when she was notified by her Series 6 Apple Watch© (version 9.6.3) that her oxygen level was low.

produced_by: The wearer has an Apple Watch with the Blood Oxygen app and reviews its readings
A hypoxemic condition produces a persistently low reading at home
The wearer reports the reading and a clinician acts on it despite normal spot oximetry
must_hold: The reading is not dismissed as artifact
Confirmatory testing (CT angiography, co-oximetry) is available
Effective treatment exists for the condition found

echoes.setting: 71-year-old woman, emergency department, USA (authors' institution: University at Buffalo); her watch notified her of low oxygen and read 73–86% over the next 24 hours, but she ignored the alert and sought care only when her family saw blue discoloration of her skin; hospital pulse oximetry itself read 84% and venous methaemoglobin was 19.8% from phenazopyridine; methylene blue, discharged after about 24 hours; the watch readings corroborated the hospital finding rather than bringing her to care, so the index mechanism did not repeat (publication date)
echoes.source: Tulisiak et al. (2025). J Med Toxicol 21(4):430-433. https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12511463

paired_incident.basis: Same device, Apple Watch: a sensor-driven alert that was false (Crash Detection dialed 911 for skiers) mirrors a sensor reading that was true (88% SpO2 prompting CT); harmed were Apple Watch users and dispatchers.

fields.account: A case appeared online on 5 September 2022 in QJM (event date not reported). A 50-year-old woman who recently had COVID-19 was referred to the authors' hospital (Oita University, Yufu, Japan) for assessment of dyspnea. Hospital pulse oximetry read 97%, but her Apple Watch Series 7 had shown 88% oxygen saturation in the early morning. Prompted by the watch reading, clinicians did emergent computed tomography (CT) angiography. It showed filling defects in multiple pulmonary artery branches, confirming pulmonary embolism with bilateral deep venous thrombosis (DVT). She was treated with a direct oral anticoagulant, oxygen was stopped on day 6 and she was discharged on day 15. The authors state the watch's low reading led to the diagnosis.
